name: Gaddang
catalog_citation: Troyer, Madeline. 1959. Gaddang phonology. Philippine Journal of Science 88(1):95-102.
catalog_locator: p. 98, section 1.4 'Stress' and footnote 10 (PDF p. 104 of the whole-issue scan); p. 99, section 3.1 'Words' (PDF p. 105)
catalog_quote: STRESS. 1.4. Primary stress is not predictable in terms of any phonological feature.(10) When words are spoken in isolation, primary stress may move from syllable to syllable; the position of primary stress is therefore determined by examining words in a larger context. Examples: mətákaw 'will steal', mattakáw 'will borrow', palátaŋ 'jaw bone', matarabáfo 'will work'. A secondary stress occurs on the first syllable of four or five syllable words, and since always predictable, it is non-phonemic. Examples: [mábbalafíŋgan] mabbalafíŋgan 'will become numb', [ʔálifámbaŋ] ʔalifámbaŋ 'butterfly', [mákkakaráyyəm] makkakaráyyəm 'will visit (many)', sàlawínit salawínit 'trousers'. [fn. 10:] Primary stress occurs more frequently on the penult.
world_status: statement found in a copy we already had

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress is phonemic and lexically determined (not predictable from any phonological property); it falls most often on the penult but also on the final and antepenult (examples: mətákaw penult, mattakáw final, palátaŋ penult, matarabáfo penult of a 5-syllable word). Each phonological word (1-5 syllables) carries exactly one primary stress (sec. 3.1, p. 99).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Predictable, non-phonemic secondary stress on the first syllable of four- and five-syllable words, e.g. [mábbalafíŋgan] 'will become numb', [ʔálifámbaŋ] 'butterfly', [mákkakaráyyəm] 'will visit (many)', sàlawínit 'trousers' (p. 98).
new_statements.exceptions: None as such; the author notes that in isolation primary stress 'may move from syllable to syllable', so placement is established from words in larger context. Practical orthography (p. 101, 4(3)) writes stress only where two words would otherwise be identical.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level: the phonological word (1-5 syllables, one primary stress, pronounceable in isolation, p. 99). The author says isolated citation forms show unstable stress and that context was used to fix it; phrase/sentence intonation explicitly not studied (p. 95). Based on one principal informant (Lucio Lappao, Butigui, Bontoc = Paracelis), data 1957-58, upland 'pagan Gaddang' = Ga'dang.
new_statements.identity_note: Troyer 1959 is titled 'Gaddang phonology' but describes the upland 'pagan Gaddang' of Butigui, Bontoc (now Paracelis, Mountain Province), whose self-designation she gives as 'Gàdang' (fn. 1) -- i.e. Ga'dang gada1258, not the Christianized lowland Gaddang of Nueva Vizcaya/Isabela (gadd1244). Glottolog links the reference (id 161633) to gada1258 / [gdg]. The same scan is also held by the project, where it was first downloaded; the gadd1244 entry should NOT reuse this statement as its own. Single principal informant, 1957-58 data.

sources.note: Sec. 1.4 STRESS (p. 98): primary stress is phonemic and 'not predictable in terms of any phonological feature'; footnote 10: it 'occurs more frequently on the penult'; predictable non-phonemic secondary stress on the first syllable of 4-5-syllable words; sec. 3.1 (p. 99) defines the phonological word as having a single primary stress; sec. 4(3) (p. 101) practical orthography marks stress only to separate minimal pairs. Informant from Butigui, Bontoc (= Paracelis) = 'pagan Gaddangs' = Ga'dang; Glottolog files this article under gada1258 (ref 161633, confirmed on the Glottolog reference page).…
